cards.front: The immune proteins that coat targets so phagocytes can swallow them are called {{c1::complement}}.
cards.back: Complement helps mark targets for engulfment.
cards.quote: Complement is a set of proteins best known from the blood.

cards.front: Which resident brain cells are its main phagocytes?
cards.back: Microglia.
cards.quote: The obvious suspects for the second are microglia, the brain's resident immune cells and its main phagocytes.
cards.section: Two eyes, one relay: which inputs lose?

cards.front: What is eye-specific segregation in the developing mouse dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN)?
cards.back: Initially overlapping inputs from the two eyes sort into separate territories, mostly between about P3 and P10.
cards.quote: they sort into separate territories, a process called eye-specific segregation.
cards.section: Two eyes, one relay: which inputs lose?

cards.front: Why can retinal input refinement in mouse dLGN continue after eye territories have separated?
cards.back: Territory sorting and reducing the number of retinal inputs onto each relay neuron are distinct; the latter continues for weeks after sorting.
cards.quote: A single relay neuron also goes from many retinal inputs to a few, a refinement that continues for weeks after the territories have sorted.
cards.section: Two eyes, one relay: which inputs lose?

cards.front: How does C1q binding lead to a surface-bound complement tag?
cards.back: C1q binding activates C1r, which activates C1s; C1s cuts C4 and C2 to assemble C3 convertase. It cleaves C3, generating C3b that can attach to nearby surfaces.
cards.quote: C1s cuts C4 and C2, and the pieces assemble into an enzyme, a C3 convertase, that cuts C3 into a small fragment, C3a, and a large one, C3b.
cards.section: A tag from the immune system

cards.front: Complement receptor 3 (CR3) recognizes {{c1::iC3b}}, a trimmed form of C3b.
cards.back: CR3 binds iC3b, promoting engulfment of the coated target.
cards.quote: A phagocyte carrying complement receptor 3 (CR3) binds iC3b, which promotes engulfment of what it coats.
cards.section: A tag from the immune system

cards.front: What does a whole-body knockout disrupt?
cards.back: Both copies of one gene in every cell.
cards.quote: In a whole-body knockout mouse, both copies of one gene are disrupted in every cell.
cards.section: A tag from the immune system

cards.front: Why does a fixed image of a tagged small synaptic contact fail to prove that the contact will be eliminated?
cards.back: A fixed image cannot follow the contact over time to establish its later fate.
cards.quote: That was a proposal: fixed images could not show which contacts later disappeared.
cards.section: A tag from the immune system

cards.front: Why is the cellular source of C1q at mouse dLGN synapses still unsettled?
cards.back: Retinal neurons can express C1q, but microglia make most brain C1q; those findings do not identify the supplier at dLGN synapses.
cards.quote: Later work found that microglia make most of the C1q in the mouse brain, so which cell supplies the C1q at dLGN synapses is not settled.
cards.section: A tag from the immune system

cards.front: A mouse cannot produce C1q. As its dLGN matures, what changes are expected in eye territories and retinal convergence onto relay cells, and why?
cards.back: More persistent eye-territory overlap and several retained inputs on many relay neurons, because C1q contributes to normal refinement.
cards.quote: In mice lacking C1q, the two eyes' territories failed to refine normally and still overlapped more than in normal littermates.
cards.section: A tag from the immune system

cards.front: In a mouse dLGN slice, stronger optic-tract stimulation produces three discrete recruitment steps in a relay neuron's current. What minimum input count is supported, and why might it be low?
cards.back: At least three retinal axons contributed: each new step indicates another recruited axon. Weak inputs may be missed, so the actual input count could be higher.
cards.quote: each new step in the current marks one more retinal axon recruited. Weak inputs can be missed, so this is an estimate, not a full count.
cards.section: A tag from the immune system

cards.front: Why divide internalized retinal-label volume by microglial-cell volume when measuring engulfment?
cards.back: To prevent a larger cell from appearing to engulf more simply because it is larger.
cards.quote: Dividing by the cell's volume means a large cell does not seem to eat more merely because it is large.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: What imaging evidence distinguishes engulfed retinal material from label merely beside mouse dLGN microglia?
cards.back: Three-dimensional reconstructions located retinal label inside microglia, including their lysosomes; acid-sensitive dye and a genetic retinal label supported the result.
cards.quote: They rebuilt each microglial cell in three dimensions and kept only the label inside it. Retinal material sat inside microglial lysosomes, the cell's digestive compartments.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: Which side of the retinal synapse supplied most material detected inside developing mouse dLGN microglia?
cards.back: The presynaptic side, supported by electron microscopy and retinal-terminal protein staining.
cards.quote: Electron microscopy and staining for VGlut2, a protein of retinal terminals, showed that the engulfed material was mainly presynaptic.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: How does the timing of mouse dLGN engulfment support a role in eye-specific segregation?
cards.back: Engulfment is high at P5 during segregation and much lower by P9. This timing fits participation in sorting without establishing what sets the decline.
cards.quote: It was high at P5, when segregation is under way, and much lower by P9.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: A mouse group lacks either C3 or CR3. Compared with normal mice, what early engulfment and later wiring changes are expected in its dLGN, and why?
cards.back: Roughly half the normal uptake at P5, then more eye-territory overlap and more retinal synapses about a month after birth. C3 supplies complement tags and CR3 reads them, supporting part of engulfment.
cards.quote: Those mice later had more overlap between the eye territories, and more retinal synapses about a month after birth.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: Why can halving a microglial engulfment index at one age not predict the fraction of inputs ultimately retained?
cards.back: The index measures cargo present at one time, not cumulative inputs removed. Remaining uptake and other engulfing cells also contribute.
cards.quote: The index is a snapshot of cargo at P5, not a count of inputs removed,
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: In an invented retinal-label measurement, a microglial cell has volume 800 cubic micrometres and contains 4 cubic micrometres of retinal label. Calculate its engulfment index.
cards.back: Index = internal label volume / cell volume × 100 = 4 / 800 × 100 = 0.5%.
cards.quote: engulfment index = (volume of retinal label inside a microglial cell) ÷ (volume of that microglial cell) × 100
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: In an invented two-eye tracer experiment, local input is 80 units from eye A and 20 from eye B. Microglia contain 8 units from A and 4 from B. Which eye is preferentially engulfed after normalization, and by what factor?
cards.back: A: 8/80 = 0.10 (10%); B: 4/20 = 0.20 (20%). B is engulfed twice as much per unit available input: 0.20/0.10 = 2.
cards.quote: So compare each eye with its own input, matched or measured where the microglia are sampled.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: Tetrodotoxin (TTX) silences neurons by blocking {{c1::sodium channels}}.
cards.back: Blocking sodium channels silences neuronal activity.
cards.quote: Tetrodotoxin (TTX) blocks sodium channels and silences neurons.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: In a young mouse, forskolin raises cAMP and boosts activity in one eye. With each eye's engulfed material normalized to its local input, which eye should contribute relatively more to dLGN microglial cargo, and why?
cards.back: The untreated eye, because it is relatively less active. In this circuit microglial engulfment is biased toward the less active eye.
cards.quote: With one eye boosted, they took relatively more from the untreated eye.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: In a two-input system, silencing one input increases its normalized engulfment, while boosting it shifts engulfment toward the untreated input. Why is this pair of results stronger evidence for activity dependence than either result alone?
cards.back: Opposite activity changes shift uptake in opposite directions, following relative activity. Under the simple damage explanation, both treatments would instead increase uptake of their own treated input.
cards.quote: The two drugs push in opposite directions, which is stronger evidence than either alone: a drug that simply damaged axons would raise engulfment of its own eye both times.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: A study finds neuronal material inside phagocytes and later fewer synapses. Does combining these findings establish that engulfment initiated synapse removal? Explain the remaining alternative.
cards.back: No. Internal cargo and a later wiring endpoint do not establish the initiating event. The stated limitation is that phagocytes might instead clear material neurons have already shed.
cards.quote: these experiments do not say whether eating starts the removal or clears material that neurons shed.
cards.section: Caught in the act: microglia take the quieter eye

cards.front: How would you test whether CR3 is required for the activity bias in mouse dLGN engulfment, rather than merely for total uptake?
cards.back: Compare one-eye TTX versus control-eye uptake normalized to each eye's locally available labelled input in normal and CR3-knockout mice. Test whether the between-eye bias changes with genotype; loss of bias supports a requirement, provided residual uptake permits measurement.
cards.quote: Then ask whether the bias differs by genotype (in statistical terms, a genotype-by-treatment interaction).
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A CR3-knockout mouse still shows greater normalized uptake from its silenced eye. Can you conclude that complement tags carry no activity information?
cards.back: No. The bias can be expressed without CR3, but deleting the receptor leaves complement tags in place; another receptor could support the surviving bias.
cards.quote: A surviving bias could ride on another receptor, and losing CR3 leaves the complement tags in place.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An activity-silencing treatment increases uptake of the treated neuronal input. What control is needed to distinguish an activity effect from clearance of injured neurons?
cards.back: Check that the treatment does not kill the neurons. Dying cells could be engulfed because of injury rather than reduced activity.
cards.quote: that it does not kill retinal ganglion cells, since dying cells would be eaten for a different reason.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After deleting a candidate engulfment protein, uptake is almost undetectable and no preference between inputs is detected. What prevents a firm conclusion that the protein determines preference?
cards.back: Too little remaining uptake may make a bias impossible to measure. The stated control requires enough residual uptake before interpreting loss of preference.
cards.quote: Check that enough uptake remains in the knockouts to measure a bias.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What distinguishes a find-me signal from an eat-me signal for a phagocyte?
cards.back: Find-me signals draw phagocytes in, as ATP from damaged cells does; eat-me signals mark targets, as complement or exposed phosphatidylserine does.
cards.quote: "Find me" signals draw the eater in; "eat me" signals mark the target.
cards.section: Find me, eat me

cards.front: How can phosphatidylserine exposure change how phagocytes recognize a membrane?
cards.back: Phosphatidylserine is normally on the inner membrane face. Exposure on the outer face makes it an eat-me signal recognized by phagocytes.
cards.quote: A dying cell moves it to the outer face, where phagocytes recognize it.
cards.section: Find me, eat me

cards.front: The microglial receptor for neuronal fractalkine (CX3CL1) is {{c1::CX3CR1}}.
cards.back: CX3CR1 is the microglial receptor for fractalkine, which can be cut free from the neuronal membrane.
cards.quote: Fractalkine, also called CX3CL1, is a membrane protein on neurons that can be cut free; its receptor, CX3CR1, is on microglia.
cards.section: Find me, eat me

cards.front: Young CX3CR1-knockout mice have extra hippocampal spines, but the excess disappears by about P40. How should pruning be interpreted, and why?
cards.back: As delayed in that region rather than absent, because the excess is transient and later resolves.
cards.quote: The excess was transient, so the result is best read as delayed pruning in that region, not its absence.
cards.section: Find me, eat me

cards.front: CX3CR1 loss reduces microglial numbers in developing mouse hippocampus, but blocks engulfment without blocking recruitment in mouse barrel cortex. What does combining these observations imply about calling CX3CR1 a find-me receptor?
cards.back: The label depends on circuit and age. Hippocampal findings do not make it universal; preserved recruitment with lost engulfment in barrel cortex shows a role in eating rather than arrival.
cards.quote: its loss blocked engulfment without blocking recruitment, so there the find-me label does not hold: the receptor was needed for eating, not for arrival.
cards.section: Find me, eat me

cards.front: Why does phosphatidylserine on a developing mouse dLGN synapse not necessarily mean its entire neuron is dying?
cards.back: A synapse can expose the signal locally while its neuron lives; caspase-3 loss did not significantly change the measured synaptic signal.
cards.quote: So a synapse can display a death signal locally while its neuron lives.
cards.section: Find me, eat me

cards.front: What human genetic association links C4A to schizophrenia risk?
cards.back: Variants predicted to raise brain C4A expression were associated with higher schizophrenia risk.
cards.quote: Variants predicted to raise C4A expression in the brain were associated with a higher risk of schizophrenia.
cards.section: When pruning goes wrong: links, not causes

cards.front: Higher predicted human brain C4A expression is associated with schizophrenia risk, while mouse C4 loss reduces dLGN pruning. What joint hypothesis is supported, and what limits it?
cards.back: More complement activity might increase pruning and contribute to risk. This remains a hypothesis: human association is not causation, common variants have modest effects, and mouse visual thalamus is not human cortex.
cards.quote: The human result is an association, the common C4 variants each change risk only modestly,
cards.section: When pruning goes wrong: links, not causes

cards.front: A study finds altered synapse numbers in people with autism. Does this observation alone establish abnormal pruning as the cause of autism?
cards.back: No. Altered synapse numbers provide an association. The proposed contribution of abnormal pruning remains a hypothesis without evidence establishing causation.
cards.quote: These are hypotheses, supported by associations, and the disorders themselves are covered in the lesson on disorders of the synapse.
cards.section: When pruning goes wrong: links, not causes

cards.front: Why is microglial engulfment not the only route for synapse removal in mouse visual thalamus?
cards.back: Astrocytes also engulf synapses there, using MEGF10 and MERTK receptors.
cards.quote: in the mouse visual thalamus they engulf synapses through the receptors MEGF10 and MERTK.
cards.section: Who does the eating

cards.front: How does a quadripartite view of the synapse help explain why disrupting one microglial engulfment route need not abolish synapse removal?
cards.back: It includes presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, astrocytes and microglia. Combining this view with the stated residual uptake and astrocytic engulfment means a single microglial pathway is only part of the removal machinery.
cards.quote: Adding the microglial process that touches it and can remove it gives what can be called the "quadripartite" synapse.
cards.section: Who does the eating

cards.front: In a proposed mouse dLGN experiment, a treatment selectively strengthens the protective CD47–SIRPα signal without other changes. What should happen to engulfment, and why?
cards.back: Engulfment should decrease, because the stated role of this protective signal in mouse dLGN is to limit engulfment.
cards.quote: Candidate protective "don't eat me" signals such as CD47 and its receptor SIRPα (shown to limit engulfment in the mouse dLGN)
cards.section: Candidates for the mark

cards.front: What key mechanism remains unknown between relative retinal activity and biased microglial engulfment?
cards.back: How relative activity becomes a molecular mark; proposed protective signals, complement regulators and phosphatidylserine exposure are not yet a settled circuit-specific mechanism.
cards.quote: How relative activity becomes a molecular mark is the central open question.
cards.section: Candidates for the mark
